def show_math(latex):
    """Print a display equation from a chunk marked `output: asis`."""
    print(f"$${latex}$$\n")


def tidy(obj, digits=4):
    """Round the numbers in a result for display, leaving text, whole
    numbers, and True/False alone."""
    def r(v):
        if isinstance(v, (bool, np.bool_)):
            return bool(v)
        if isinstance(v, (float, np.floating)):
            if np.isnan(v):
                return ""
            return int(v) if float(v).is_integer() and abs(v) >= 1 else round(float(v), digits)
        return v
    if isinstance(obj, pd.DataFrame):
        return obj.astype(object).apply(lambda col: col.map(r))
    return obj.astype(object).map(r)


def numbers(series, digits=4):
    """A result Series as a one-column table."""
    return tidy(series, digits).to_frame("value")

## Objectives

+ Explain the chi-square statistic as a measure of how far observed counts
  sit from the counts a hypothesis predicts, and find its p-value.
+ Test whether **k proportions** are equal, and recognize the $2\times2$
  case as last week's two-proportion test.
+ Test whether counts follow a stated distribution (**goodness of fit**),
  including the degrees-of-freedom cost of estimating a parameter.
+ Test whether two categorical variables are **independent**, find which
  cells drive a rejection, and measure how strong the association is.
+ Know when expected counts are too small, and how to combine categories.
+ Test a single population variance, and build an interval for $\sigma$.
+ Compare two population variances with the $F$ test.
+ Explain why the variance tests need normal data much more than the
  $t$-test does, and what to do instead of pretesting variances.

::: {.charcoal}
Weeks 9 and 10 tested claims about **means and proportions**. This week has
two new questions.

**Chapter 12: do counts match a hypothesis?** Is the share of "up" days the
same every weekday? Do absences follow a Poisson model? Does the brand a
customer buys depend on age? Every one of these is answered with one
statistic,

$$\chi^2=\sum_{\text{cells}}\frac{(\text{observed}-\text{expected})^2}{\text{expected}},$$

and the three tests in the chapter differ only in **where the expected counts
come from**. Learn the statistic once, then learn three ways of filling in
"expected."

**Chapter 13: is the spread what was claimed?** A refrigerator can average
37°F and still freeze the lettuce. A checkout process can average 4 minutes
and still leave some customers waiting 10. Here the parameter of interest is
the variance $\sigma^2$, and the test has an important catch that the
$t$-test does not.
:::

# Part I: Chi-Square Tests (Chapter 12)

## The chi-square statistic

::: {.blue}
For counts in $k$ cells, the **chi-square statistic** is

$$\chi^2=\sum\frac{(f_o-f_e)^2}{f_e},$$

where $f_o$ is the **observed** count in a cell and $f_e$ is the
**expected** count if $H_0$ is true. Expected counts need not be whole
numbers; they are averages.

If $H_0$ is true, $\chi^2$ follows (approximately) a **chi-square
distribution**, which is right-skewed, never negative, and has mean equal to
its degrees of freedom. The approximation needs **every expected count to be
at least 5**; if one is not, combine categories.
:::

```{python}
#| label: chi2-curves
cx = np.linspace(0.01, 20, 600)
_ = density_chart(cx, {"df = 1": chi2_pdf(cx, 1), "df = 2": chi2_pdf(cx, 2),
                       "df = 4": chi2_pdf(cx, 4), "df = 8": chi2_pdf(cx, 8)},
                  title="Chi-square distributions: right-skewed, mean = df",
                  xlab="chi-square", ymax=0.5)
```

::: {.charcoal}
Three things follow from the formula.

+ **Every test is upper-tailed.** Squaring makes a cell count too high and a
  cell count too low both add to $\chi^2$. Only a *large* $\chi^2$ is
  evidence against $H_0$, so the p-value is always the right-tail area,
  Excel's `=CHISQ.DIST.RT(x, df)`.
+ **Each cell's contribution is scaled by what was expected.** Being 10 off
  when 20 were expected matters more than being 10 off when 200 were.
+ **A quick sanity check:** since the mean is the df, a $\chi^2$ near its df is
  entirely ordinary. A value of 5 with 4 df is nothing; a value of 30 with 4
  df is a lot.
:::

We can check that the chi-square distribution really describes the
statistic. Below, a model with six categories is assumed true, 240
observations are drawn from it 20,000 times, and $\chi^2$ is computed each
time.

```{python}
#| label: chi2-sim
drive_p = [0.20, 0.10, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.20]
sim = simulate_chi2_null(drive_p, 240, reps=20_000)
_ = density_histogram(sim[sim < 20], x=cx, density=chi2_pdf(cx, 5), bins=60,
                      title="20,000 chi-square statistics when H0 is true (k = 6)",
                      xlab="chi-square", curve_label="chi-square, df = 5",
                      bar_label="simulated")
```

```{python}
#| label: chi2-sim-stats
#| include: false
sim_mean = sim.mean()
sim_tail = (sim > chi2_inv(0.95, 5)).mean()
```

::: {.charcoal}
The simulated statistics average `{python} f"{sim_mean:.2f}"`, against the
df of 5, and `{python} pct(sim_tail, 1)` of them exceed the 5% critical
value. The formula's distribution is the right one, provided the expected
counts are large enough. Here the smallest is 24.
:::

## Test 1: are k proportions equal?

::: {.blue}
To test $H_0:p_1=p_2=\cdots=p_k$, pool all the groups to estimate the common
proportion $\bar{p}$, and expect $\bar{p}\times n_j$ successes (and
$(1-\bar{p})\times n_j$ failures) in group $j$. The statistic has
$\text{df}=k-1$.
:::

### Application: is Monday the best day on Wall Street?

A 2010 *Bloomberg BusinessWeek* article declared that "on Wall Street,
Monday is the best day of the week": over six months, the S&P 500 rose on
80% of Mondays, more than on any other weekday. Your textbook tests the
article's own data.

```{python}
#| label: sp-book
book_up = [20, 15, 17, 14, 12]
book_n = [25, 26, 26, 25, 23]
days = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"]
sp_tab, sp_res = k_proportions_test(book_up, book_n, days)
tidy(sp_tab, 3)
```

```{python}
#| label: sp-book-res
numbers(sp_res)
```

```{python}
#| label: sp-book-chart
_ = test_chart(cx, chi2_pdf(cx, 4), sp_res["chi-square statistic"],
               critical=sp_res["critical value"], alternative="greater",
               p_value=sp_res["p-value"],
               title="Six months of S&P days: chi-square with 4 df, if H0 is true",
               xlab="chi-square")
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{sp_res['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"` with 4 df, a
perfectly ordinary value, and $p=$ `{python} f"{sp_res['p-value']:.3f}"`. The
80% of Mondays sounds impressive, but with about 25 days per weekday, a gap
that size turns up by chance more than a quarter of the time. **The data are
not evidence that the share of up days differs by weekday.** (Your textbook
gets 5.09; it rounds each expected count before adding.)
:::

The course repository has ten years of daily S&P 500 closes from FRED,
August 2016 to August 2026. An up day is a close above the previous day's
close.

```{python}
#| label: sp-fred
spd = sp.sort_values("date").copy()
spd["up"] = spd["sp500_close"].diff() > 0
spd = spd.iloc[1:]
spd["weekday"] = pd.Categorical(spd["date"].dt.day_name(), days, ordered=True)
counts = spd.groupby("weekday", observed=True)["up"].agg(["sum", "size"])
counts.columns = ["up days", "trading days"]
counts["share up"] = counts["up days"] / counts["trading days"]
fred_tab, fred_res = k_proportions_test(counts["up days"], counts["trading days"], days)
counts.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: sp-fred-res
numbers(fred_res)
```

::: {.charcoal}
Over `{python} f"{int(counts['trading days'].sum()):,}"` trading days,
Monday again has the highest share of up days,
`{python} pct(counts.loc['Monday', 'share up'], 1)`, against
`{python} pct(counts['share up'].min(), 1)` for the lowest weekday. With twenty
times the data, $\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{fred_res['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"`
and $p=$ `{python} f"{fred_res['p-value']:.3f}"`. Still no evidence of a
weekday effect. A pattern that "everyone knows" and that a reputable
magazine printed is, as far as these data can tell, noise. This is the use
of statistics most worth taking into a business career.
:::

### The $2\times2$ case is last week's test

With only two groups, the chi-square test of equal proportions **is** the
two-proportion $z$-test of Chapter 10: $\chi^2=z^2$, with the same p-value.
Take last week's email A/B test (216 of 2,400 bought after email B, 168 of
2,400 after email A):

```{python}
#| label: chi-z
ab_tab, ab_chi = k_proportions_test([216, 168], [2400, 2400], ["email B", "email A"])
ab_z = two_proportion_test(216, 2400, 168, 2400)
pd.Series({"z (Chapter 10)": ab_z["test statistic z"],
           "z squared": ab_z["test statistic z"] ** 2,
           "chi-square (this week)": ab_chi["chi-square statistic"],
           "p-value, z test": ab_z["p-value"],
           "p-value, chi-square": ab_chi["p-value"]}).round(4).to_frame("value")
```

::: {.charcoal}
Same test, same answer. The chi-square version extends to any number of
groups; the $z$ version can also be one-tailed ("B is *better*"), which a
chi-square test cannot, because squaring throws the direction away.
:::

## Test 2: goodness of fit

::: {.blue}
A **goodness-of-fit test** asks whether observed counts follow a stated
probability distribution. $H_0$ says they do. The expected count in each
category is $n\times$ the probability the model gives it, and

$$\text{df}=k-m-1,$$

where $k$ is the number of categories and $m$ is the number of parameters
**estimated from the sample** to compute those probabilities ($m=0$ if $H_0$
states the model completely). Each estimated parameter lets the model
bend toward the data, and costs one degree of freedom.
:::

### Application: a fully stated distribution

A bank's managers believe drive-through demand is spread across the week as
20%, 10%, 10%, 15%, 25%, 20% (Monday to Saturday). One week brings 240
customers. Test at $\alpha=0.05$.

```{python}
#| label: drive
drive_tab, drive_res = gof_test([58, 21, 27, 20, 71, 43], drive_p,
                                ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat"],
                                m=0, alpha=0.05)
tidy(drive_tab, 3)
```

```{python}
#| label: drive-res
numbers(drive_res.drop(labels=["CHISQ.TEST"]))
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{drive_res['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"` with
$6-0-1=5$ df, $p=$ `{python} f"{drive_res['p-value']:.4f}"`: **the data are
evidence that demand does not follow the stated pattern.** The working table
shows where: Thursday contributes more than half of the statistic on its own
(20 customers against 36 expected). That is the staffing question to take
back to the managers.
:::

### Application: a Poisson model with $\lambda$ estimated

Absences per class meeting in 150 meetings:

```{python}
#| label: absent-data
absent_vals = list(range(7))
absent_freq = [22, 38, 39, 29, 15, 5, 2]
pd.DataFrame({"students absent": absent_vals, "class meetings": absent_freq}).set_index("students absent").T
```

$H_0$ says absences follow *a* Poisson distribution, without stating its
mean. So $\lambda$ must be estimated from the data,
$\bar{x}=300/150=2.0$, and that costs a degree of freedom. The Poisson
probability of 6 or more is small enough that its expected count falls below
5, so "5" and "6 or more" are merged into "5 or more."

```{python}
#| label: absent
pois_tab, pois_res = poisson_gof(absent_vals, absent_freq, top=5)
tidy(pois_tab, 3)
```

```{python}
#| label: absent-res
numbers(pois_res.drop(labels=["CHISQ.TEST"]))
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\lambda=$ `{python} f"{pois_res['lambda']:.1f}"`, six categories, one
estimated parameter: $\text{df}=6-1-1=4$. $\chi^2=$
`{python} f"{pois_res['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"` and $p=$
`{python} f"{pois_res['p-value']:.2f}"`. **The data are consistent with a
Poisson model.**
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Two cautions.**

1. **A large p-value does not show that the model is right.** It shows the
   data cannot tell the model apart from the truth. Using the Poisson to plan
   an attendance policy may be a sensible business decision, but this test
   did not prove the data are Poisson. Your textbook goes further than the
   evidence when it says there is "more evidence supporting the use of the
   Poisson distribution than there is to not use it."
2. **Excel's `CHISQ.TEST` gets the df wrong here.** `=CHISQ.TEST(observed,
   expected)` always uses $k-1$ degrees of freedom. That is right for the
   drive-through ($m=0$) and wrong whenever a parameter was estimated: here
   it would use 5 df instead of 4. Use `=CHISQ.DIST.RT(chi-square, k-m-1)`.
:::

::: {.brown}
**Southwest's late flights.** Southwest flies four flights a day between
Philadelphia and Orlando. Over 200 days, the number of late flights per day
was 0 on 70 days, 1 on 78 days, 2 on 40 days, and 3 or 4 on 12 days.
Nationally, 20% of Southwest flights are late. **(a)** Test at
$\alpha=0.05$ whether late flights per day follow a binomial distribution
with $n=4$ and $p=0.2$. **(b)** How many degrees of freedom, and why?
**(c)** The model fails. Look at *where* it fails, and suggest why. (Hint:
which binomial assumption does the weather violate?)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: southwest
sw_tab, sw_res = binomial_gof([0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [70, 78, 40, 12, 0], n=4, top=3,
                              p=0.20, alpha=0.05)
sw_tab.index = ["0", "1", "2", "3 or 4", "Total"]
tidy(sw_tab, 2)
```

**(a)** $\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{sw_res['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"`, $p=$
`{python} f"{sw_res['p-value']:.4f}"`: reject. The counts do not follow
Binomial(4, 0.2). **(b)** Four categories after merging "3" and "4" (the
expected count for 4 alone is 0.32); $p$ was stated, so $m=0$ and
$\text{df}=4-0-1=3$. **(c)** There are too many days with **no** late
flights (70 against 82 expected) and far too many with **3 or 4** (12
against 5.4). The binomial assumes the four flights are *independent*. They
are not: a thunderstorm in Orlando delays every flight that day, and a clear
day delays none. Dependence between trials pushes days toward the extremes,
which is exactly the pattern here. Your textbook concludes only that
Southwest "needs to develop another model," and its sentence is garbled ("By
rejecting the null hypothesis, we have no evidence to conclude that … follows
the binomial"). Rejecting H₀ *is* the evidence that the binomial does not
fit.
:::

::: {.brown}
**Is it normal?** Your textbook also tests normality this way, by cutting the
$z$-scale into intervals (Section 12.2). With 40 observations it can afford
only four intervals, leaving **1 degree of freedom**, and such a test will
miss almost any departure from normality. Read the section for the method.
In practice, look at the data: the tail check from Chapter 6 (what share of
values lie beyond $\pm2$ and $\pm3$ standard deviations, against the normal's
4.6% and 0.27%), a histogram, or a normal probability plot. Part II shows why
this matters.
:::

## Test 3: are two categorical variables independent?

::: {.blue}
A **contingency table** cross-classifies $n$ observations by two categorical
variables, with $r$ rows and $c$ columns. The **test of independence** has

$$H_0:\ \text{the row and column variables are independent},$$

and, if $H_0$ is true, the expected count in a cell is

$$f_e=\frac{(\text{row total})\times(\text{column total})}{n},
\qquad \text{df}=(r-1)(c-1).$$
:::

::: {.charcoal}
**Where the formula comes from.** Chapter 4 said events $A$ and $B$ are
independent when $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)\,P(B)$. Estimate each probability
from the margins, $P(\text{row})=\text{row total}/n$ and
$P(\text{column})=\text{column total}/n$, and multiply by $n$:
$n\cdot\frac{\text{row}}{n}\cdot\frac{\text{column}}{n}=\frac{\text{row}\times\text{column}}{n}$.
Read it another way: if the column a customer falls in has nothing to do with
the row, every row should split across the columns in the same proportions
as the whole sample does. The test of independence is Chapter 4's
definition, checked with data.
:::

### Application: does camera brand depend on age?

A Best Buy store records the brand and the age group of 150 digital camera
buyers.

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy
bestbuy = pd.DataFrame({"Canon": [30, 22, 8], "Nikon": [16, 25, 9],
                        "Sony": [8, 19, 13]},
                       index=pd.Index(["18-34", "35-51", "52+"], name="age"))
bb = independence_test(bestbuy)
shown = bestbuy.copy()
shown["Total"] = shown.sum(axis=1)
shown.loc["Total"] = shown.sum()
shown
```

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-math
#| output: asis
_r, _c, _n = bestbuy.loc["18-34"].sum(), bestbuy["Canon"].sum(), bestbuy.values.sum()
show_math(rf"f_e(\text{{18-34, Canon}})=\frac{{{_r}\times{_c}}}{{{_n}}}"
          rf"={bb['expected'].loc['18-34', 'Canon']:.1f}")
```

The expected counts for every cell, if brand and age are independent:

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-exp
bb["expected"].round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-res
numbers(bb["result"])
```

::: {.charcoal}
Every expected count is at least
`{python} f"{bb['result']['smallest expected count']:.0f}"`, so the
approximation is fine. $\chi^2=$
`{python} f"{bb['result']['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"` with
$(3-1)(3-1)=4$ df, $p=$ `{python} f"{bb['result']['p-value']:.4f}"`: **the
data are evidence that brand choice and age are related.**
:::

### Where is the dependence? Standardized residuals

A rejection says only that *somewhere* the table departs from independence.
To find where, look at each cell's **standardized residual**,

$$\frac{f_o-f_e}{\sqrt{f_e}}.$$

Squared, these are exactly the pieces that add up to $\chi^2$. Read them
like $z$-scores: beyond about $\pm2$ is a cell that clearly departs from
independence, and beyond $\pm1.5$ is worth a look.

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-resid
bb["residuals"].round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-resid-stats
#| include: false
bbr = bb["residuals"]
```

::: {.charcoal}
Three cells carry the result. Buyers aged 18-34 choose Canon more often than
independence predicts (residual
`{python} f"{bbr.loc['18-34', 'Canon']:+.2f}"`) and Sony less often
(`{python} f"{bbr.loc['18-34', 'Sony']:+.2f}"`); buyers 52 and over choose
Sony more often (`{python} f"{bbr.loc['52+', 'Sony']:+.2f}"`). The middle
age group looks like the store as a whole. That is the sentence a category
manager can use: where to put the Canon display, and who the Sony
promotion should target.
:::

### How strong is the dependence? Cramér's V

The $\chi^2$ statistic grows with $n$: double every count and $\chi^2$
doubles, though the pattern is unchanged. So, as in weeks 9 and 10, a small
p-value says the association is *real*, not that it is *large*. The effect
size for a contingency table is **Cramér's V**:

::: {.blue}
$$V=\sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n\,\big(\min(r,c)-1\big)}},$$

which runs from 0 (independence) to 1 (each row predicts the column
perfectly). A rough guide for tables with a shorter side of 2 or 3: about
0.1 is small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large.
:::

```{python}
#| label: bestbuy-v
#| output: asis
_v = bb["result"]
bb_v = _v["Cramer's V"]
show_math(rf"V=\sqrt{{\frac{{{_v['chi-square statistic']:.3f}}}"
          rf"{{{_v['n']:.0f}\times(3-1)}}}}={bb_v:.3f}")
```

Now a case where $n$ is large. Your textbook's *Focus on Analytics* box
reports a survey by Soliton Technologies of 2,069 people: were they the
decision maker the last time their household bought a car?

```{python}
#| label: soliton
soliton = pd.DataFrame({"Male": [207, 811], "Female": [67, 984]},
                       index=pd.Index(["Decision maker: yes", "Decision maker: no"]))
sol = independence_test(soliton)
sol_v = sol["result"]["Cramer's V"]
soliton
```

```{python}
#| label: soliton-res
numbers(sol["result"].drop(labels=["p-value"]))
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{sol['result']['chi-square statistic']:.1f}"` with 1
df, and the p-value is too small for Excel to show (well below one in a
billion). Yet $V=$ `{python} f"{sol_v:.2f}"`, about
the same as the Best Buy table, which had $p=$
`{python} f"{bb['result']['p-value']:.3f}"`. The two associations are about
**equally strong**. The Soliton p-value is tiny because $n$ is 14 times
larger. Always report the effect size next to the p-value.
:::

### Application: a physician "upcoding" check

Your textbook's box *Using the Chi-Square Test in Health Care* describes
Health Care Associates (HCA), which places hospitalists at University
Hospital. Patients are assigned to physicians at random, so a physician's
patients should have the same mix of admission levels (Level 3 is the most
complex, and the most expensive to bill). Insurers watch for **upcoding**:
classifying a Level 1 admission as Level 2 or 3 to raise revenue.

```{python}
#| label: hca
hca = pd.DataFrame([[3, 4, 9, 9, 13, 8], [15, 8, 21, 16, 13, 19],
                    [45, 27, 13, 16, 19, 32]],
                   index=["Level 1", "Level 2", "Level 3"],
                   columns=[f"Phys {i}" for i in range(1, 7)])
hc = independence_test(hca)
hca
```

```{python}
#| label: hca-res
numbers(hc["result"])
```

```{python}
#| label: hca-resid
hc["residuals"].round(2)
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{hc['result']['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"` with
$(3-1)(6-1)=10$ df, $p=$ `{python} f"{hc['result']['p-value']:.4f}"`.
Admission level is not independent of physician. The residuals point at
**Physician 1**: `{python} int(hca.loc['Level 3', 'Phys 1'])` Level 3
patients against `{python} f"{hc['expected'].loc['Level 3', 'Phys 1']:.0f}"`
expected (`{python} f"{hc['residuals'].loc['Level 3', 'Phys 1']:+.2f}"`),
and only `{python} int(hca.loc['Level 1', 'Phys 1'])` Level 1 patients against
`{python} f"{hc['expected'].loc['Level 1', 'Phys 1']:.0f}"`
(`{python} f"{hc['residuals'].loc['Level 1', 'Phys 1']:+.2f}"`). Physicians 3
and 5 lean the other way. The test does not prove anyone upcoded: the
assignment may not be as random as HCA thinks, or Physician 1 may take the
night shift when the sickest patients arrive. What it does is tell the
compliance office **which chart to pull first**. That is the business use
of residuals.
:::

### Application: small expected counts, and combining categories

The course's faculty file has the rank and sex of
`{python} len(faculty)` economics professors at nine Big Ten universities in
1999. Is rank independent of sex?

```{python}
#| label: fac-table
rank_sex = pd.crosstab(faculty["rank"], faculty["sex"])
fac = independence_test(rank_sex)
rank_sex
```

```{python}
#| label: fac-exp
fac["expected"].round(2)
```

::: {.scarlet}
**Stop before computing a p-value.** The expected counts for female
assistant and associate professors are
`{python} f"{fac['expected'].loc['Assistant', 'Female']:.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{fac['expected'].loc['Associate', 'Female']:.2f}"`, below 5. With
counts this small, the chi-square distribution is a poor approximation to
the statistic's real distribution, and the p-value it gives
(`{python} f"{fac['result']['p-value']:.4f}"`, as it happens) cannot be
trusted. Software will compute it anyway, sometimes with a warning, sometimes
not.
:::

The fix is to **combine categories** that belong together. Assistant and
associate professors are both below full professor, so merge them:

```{python}
#| label: fac-merged
rank2 = faculty["rank"].replace({"Assistant": "Assistant or Associate",
                                 "Associate": "Assistant or Associate"})
rank_sex2 = pd.crosstab(rank2, faculty["sex"])
fac2 = independence_test(rank_sex2)
pd.concat({"observed": rank_sex2, "expected": fac2["expected"].round(2)}, axis=1)
```

```{python}
#| label: fac-merged-res
numbers(fac2["result"])
```

```{python}
#| label: fac-shares
#| include: false
share_f = rank_sex2["Female"] / rank_sex2.sum(axis=1)
```

::: {.charcoal}
Every expected count is now at least
`{python} f"{fac2['result']['smallest expected count']:.1f}"`, and with
1 df, $\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{fac2['result']['chi-square statistic']:.2f}"`,
$p=$ `{python} f"{fac2['result']['p-value']:.4f}"`. Women are
`{python} pct(share_f['Assistant or Associate'], 1)` of assistant and
associate professors but `{python} pct(share_f['Professor'], 1)` of full
professors. The data are evidence that rank and sex are related in these
departments. Combine on meaning (adjacent ranks, adjacent counts, the top
values of a count variable), never by searching for the merge that gives
the smallest p-value.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Association is not causation.** Every table in this section is
observational, so the test of independence says the variables *move
together*, not *why*. Your textbook says so correctly. The faculty table
shows how much this matters. One explanation is that women were promoted
less often. Another is **timing**: if women entered economics faculties in
larger numbers only in the 1980s and 1990s, many would not yet have had the
years to reach full professor in 1999. The chi-square test cannot tell
these apart; data on hiring year and promotion would be needed. The same
caution applies to Best Buy (age might stand in for income or for
experience with a brand) and to HCA.
:::

::: {.gray}
**Three tests, one statistic.**

| Test | $H_0$ | Expected count $f_e$ | df |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $k$ proportions | $p_1=\cdots=p_k$ | $\bar{p}\,n_j$ and $(1-\bar{p})\,n_j$ | $k-1$ |
| Goodness of fit | the counts follow a stated model | $n\times$ model probability | $k-m-1$ |
| Independence | rows and columns are independent | row × column / $n$ | $(r-1)(c-1)$ |

In all three: $\chi^2=\sum(f_o-f_e)^2/f_e$, the p-value is the right tail,
and every $f_e$ should be at least 5. The $k$-proportions test is in fact a
test of independence on a $2\times k$ table (success/failure by group), so
the first and third rows always give the same answer.
:::

# Part II: Tests for a Population Variance (Chapter 13)

## One variance

::: {.blue}
If the population is **normal**, the statistic

$$\chi^2=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}$$

follows a chi-square distribution with $n-1$ df when $H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2$
is true. Unlike Chapter 12, the test can be lower-tailed, upper-tailed, or
two-tailed, depending on $H_1$. A claim about a standard deviation is tested
as a claim about its square: $\sigma<2$ minutes is $\sigma^2<4$
minutes².
:::

::: {.charcoal}
The intuition: $s^2/\sigma_0^2$ is the ratio of the variance you saw to the
variance claimed, and should be near 1 if the claim is right. Multiplying by
$n-1$ puts it on the chi-square scale, whose mean is $n-1$. A statistic far
below $n-1$ says the data are less variable than claimed; far above says more.
:::

### Application: self-serve checkout (lower tail)

A grocery chain will install self-serve checkout in more stores if the
standard deviation of self-serve checkout times is **less than 2 minutes**:
a large standard deviation would mean some customers struggle with the
machines. A pilot store times 24 self-serve customers. Test at $\alpha=0.05$:

$$H_0:\sigma^2\ge4\qquad H_1:\sigma^2<4.$$

```{python}
#| label: checkout
co = variance_test_from_data(CHECKOUT, 4.0, alternative="less")
numbers(co)
```

```{python}
#| label: checkout-math
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"\chi^2=\frac{{(n-1)s^2}}{{\sigma_0^2}}=\frac{{({co['n']}-1)"
          rf"({co['sample variance s^2']:.4f})}}{{4.0}}"
          rf"={co['chi-square statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma0^2']:.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: checkout-chart
vx = np.linspace(0.01, 50, 600)
_ = test_chart(vx, chi2_pdf(vx, 23), co["chi-square statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma0^2"],
               critical=chi2_inv(0.05, 23), alternative="less",
               p_value=co["p-value"],
               title="Checkout times: chi-square with 23 df, if sigma = 2",
               xlab="chi-square")
```

::: {.charcoal}
$s=$ `{python} f"{co['sample sd s']:.3f}"` minutes, and $\chi^2=$
`{python} f"{co['chi-square statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma0^2']:.2f}"`, well below
the df of 23. The lower-tail p-value, Excel's
`=CHISQ.DIST(x, 23, TRUE)`, is `{python} f"{co['p-value']:.4f}"`. **The
data are evidence that the standard deviation is below 2 minutes**, and by
the chain's rule the systems should go into more stores.
:::

### Application: refrigerator temperatures (two tails), and an interval for $\sigma$

Amana wants a refrigerator model whose temperature has a standard deviation
of **4.0°F**: more variation freezes or spoils food, less means the
compressor cycles too often. A test unit records 30 temperatures. Test at
$\alpha=0.05$:

$$H_0:\sigma^2=16\qquad H_1:\sigma^2\ne16.$$

```{python}
#| label: amana
am = variance_test_from_data(AMANA, 16.0, alternative="two-sided")
numbers(am)
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\chi^2=$ `{python} f"{am['chi-square statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma0^2']:.2f}"` sits
between the two critical values, and the two-sided p-value (twice the
smaller tail) is `{python} f"{am['p-value']:.3f}"`. **The data are not
evidence that the standard deviation differs from 4.0°F.**
:::

How close to 4.0°F is the standard deviation, then? A confidence interval
answers that. Because the chi-square distribution is skewed, the interval
is **not** "estimate ± margin":

::: {.blue}
For a normal population, a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval for $\sigma$ is

$$\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\ \text{upper}}}}\ \le\ \sigma\ \le\
\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\ \text{lower}}}},$$

where the two $\chi^2$ values cut off $\alpha/2$ in each tail with $n-1$ df.
In Excel they are `=CHISQ.INV.RT(alpha/2, n-1)` and `=CHISQ.INV(alpha/2, n-1)`.
:::

```{python}
#| label: amana-ci
am_ci = sigma_interval(am["sample sd s"], am["n"], 0.95)
numbers(am_ci)
```

::: {.scarlet}
**Failing to reject is not showing that $\sigma=4$.** Your textbook
concludes that "choosing to find support for the null hypothesis … is the
appropriate business decision" and that the design "is working properly."
The 95% interval says $\sigma$ could be anywhere from
`{python} f"{am_ci['lower limit for sigma']:.2f}"`°F to
`{python} f"{am_ci['upper limit for sigma']:.2f}"`°F. At the top of that range,
the refrigerator's temperature varies about 50% more than the target. Thirty
readings cannot tell a good design from a mediocre one. The business
decision might still be to ship, but the honest summary is "we found no
problem, and our test could not have found a moderate one." If the
decision matters, collect more data, and decide in advance how far from
4.0°F would be unacceptable.
:::

::: {.brown}
**Canon Business Solutions (CBS)** will hire more service staff if the
standard deviation of customer wait times for a copier repair **exceeds 30
minutes**. A random sample of 20 service calls has $s=32.4$ minutes.
**(a)** State the hypotheses and test at $\alpha=0.05$. **(b)** Find and
interpret the p-value. **(c)** Does $s>30$ mean CBS should hire?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: cbs
cbs = variance_test(32.4 ** 2, 20, 30.0 ** 2, alternative="greater", alpha=0.05)
numbers(cbs)
```

**(a)** $H_0:\sigma^2\le900$, $H_1:\sigma^2>900$ (minutes²).
$\chi^2=19(32.4^2)/900=$
`{python} f"{cbs['chi-square statistic (n-1)s^2/sigma0^2']:.2f}"`, below the
critical value
`{python} cbs['critical value(s)'].split(' ')[0]`: do not reject.
**(b)** $p=$ `{python} f"{cbs['p-value']:.3f}"`, from
`=CHISQ.DIST.RT(22.16, 19)`. If $\sigma$ were exactly 30 minutes, a sample
standard deviation at least this large would turn up in about
`{python} pct(cbs['p-value'], 0)` of samples of 20. **(c)** No. A sample
standard deviation slightly above 30 is what samples from a $\sigma=30$
population often produce; the data are not evidence that $\sigma>30$, so by
its own rule CBS does not hire. (This is not evidence that $\sigma\le30$
either.)
:::

## Two variances: the F test

::: {.blue}
For independent random samples from two **normal** populations,

$$F=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}$$

follows an $F$ distribution with $(n_1-1,\ n_2-1)$ df when
$H_0:\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2$ is true. You met this distribution in week 10's
ANOVA slice. $F$ near 1 means similar spread.

**Which population is "1" is fixed by the question, before looking at the
data.** For $H_1:\sigma_1^2>\sigma_2^2$, the p-value is the right tail,
`=F.DIST.RT(F, n1-1, n2-1)`. For $H_1:\sigma_1^2\ne\sigma_2^2$, it is twice
the smaller tail.
:::

### Application: does outsourcing make drive-through times more consistent? (one tail)

A Taco Bell owner is considering outsourcing drive-through order-taking to a
call center. His goal is **more consistent** service times. He times 12
customers under the current on-site system and 14 under a trial of the
outsourced system. The question is whether the outsourced system has the
smaller variance, so population 1 is the on-site system:

$$H_0:\sigma^2_{\text{on-site}}\le\sigma^2_{\text{outsourced}}\qquad
H_1:\sigma^2_{\text{on-site}}>\sigma^2_{\text{outsourced}}.$$

```{python}
#| label: tacobell-strip
_tb = pd.DataFrame({"seconds": ON_SITE + OUTSOURCED,
                    "system": ["on-site"] * len(ON_SITE) + ["outsourced"] * len(OUTSOURCED)})
_tb.groupby("system")["seconds"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"]).round(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: tacobell
tb = f_test_from_data(ON_SITE, OUTSOURCED, alternative="greater",
                      labels=("on-site", "outsourced"))
numbers(tb)
```

```{python}
#| label: tacobell-chart
fx = np.linspace(0.01, 5, 600)
_ = test_chart(fx, f_pdf(fx, 11, 13), tb["F = s1^2/s2^2"],
               critical=float(tb["critical value(s)"].split(" ")[0]),
               alternative="greater", p_value=tb["p-value"],
               title="Taco Bell: F with (11, 13) df, if the variances are equal",
               xlab="F")
```

::: {.charcoal}
$F=$ `{python} f"{tb['s1^2']:.1f}"` / `{python} f"{tb['s2^2']:.1f}"` $=$
`{python} f"{tb['F = s1^2/s2^2']:.3f}"`, $p=$ `{python} f"{tb['p-value']:.4f}"`.
**The data are evidence that the outsourced system gives more consistent
service times.** The outsourced mean is, if anything, a little *higher*
(`{python} f"{np.mean(OUTSOURCED):.0f}"` against
`{python} f"{np.mean(ON_SITE):.0f}"` seconds). The case for outsourcing is
entirely about spread, which a $t$-test of the means would never see.
:::

### Application: hospital stays (two tails)

Blue Cross Blue Shield (BCBS) compares the variability of the length of stay
for one procedure at two hospitals, with no prior view of which is more
variable. From 20 patients at each: Christiana $s=0.92$ days, Bayhealth
$s=0.71$ days. Test at $\alpha=0.05$.

```{python}
#| label: bcbs
bc = f_test_variances(0.92, 20, 0.71, 20, alternative="two-sided",
                      labels=("Christiana", "Bayhealth"))
numbers(bc)
```

::: {.charcoal}
$F=0.92^2/0.71^2=$ `{python} f"{bc['F = s1^2/s2^2']:.3f}"`, and the two-sided
$p=$ `{python} f"{bc['p-value']:.3f}"`, twice `=F.DIST.RT(1.679, 19, 19)`. **The
data are not evidence that the hospitals differ in variability.** Note the
units: the test is about variances (days²), so square the standard deviations
first. Your textbook warns about this, and it is the most common error in
this section.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Your textbook's rule, "always put the larger sample variance in the
numerator and do a right-tail test," is safe only for two-tailed tests.**
For a two-tailed test, larger-on-top with $\alpha/2$ in the right tail gives
exactly the p-value above. For a **one-tailed** test, it lets the data choose
the direction, the tail-picking problem from week 9. In the Taco Bell case
the question and the data happen to agree. Had the outsourced sample come out
*more* variable, the rule would have flipped the populations and tested a
question the owner never asked. Set the direction from the question. If the
data go the other way, $F<1$ and you simply do not reject.
:::

## The catch: these tests need normal data, and more data does not help

Every test in weeks 9 and 10 leaned on the Central Limit Theorem: whatever
the population's shape, $\bar{x}$ is close to normal once $n$ is large
enough. **Nothing like that rescues $s^2$.** The distribution of
$(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-square only for a normal population, and for a
skewed or heavy-tailed population it is wrong at every sample size: its
spread depends on how heavy the population's tails are.

To see how much this matters, take the course's Nevada income file,
`{python} f"{len(agi):,}"` simulated tax returns (AGI in tens of thousands of
dollars), strongly right-skewed. Treat it as the population. Draw 20,000
samples of size $n$, test the **true** variance at $\alpha=0.05$ two-sided,
and count how often the test rejects. Every rejection is a false positive,
so a valid test should reject 5% of the time. For comparison, do the same
with a $t$-test of the true mean, and with a normal population.

```{python}
#| label: robust-sim
sizes = [10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 400]
rows = []
for n_ in sizes:
    a_ = variance_test_error_rate(agi.values, n_, reps=20_000)
    z_ = variance_test_error_rate(None, n_, reps=20_000)
    rows.append({"n": n_,
                 "variance test, AGI": a_["variance test rejects a true H0"],
                 "t-test, AGI": a_["t-test rejects a true H0"],
                 "variance test, normal": z_["variance test rejects a true H0"],
                 "t-test, normal": z_["t-test rejects a true H0"]})
robust = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n")
robust.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: robust-chart
_ = line_chart(robust.index, {c: robust[c] for c in robust.columns},
               title="How often a 5% test rejects a TRUE null",
               xlab="sample size n", ylab="false-positive rate",
               hlines=[0.05], ylim=(0, 0.3))
```

::: {.charcoal}
With normal data, both tests reject about 5% of the time, as advertised. With
the skewed income data, the $t$-test starts too high
(`{python} pct(robust.loc[10, 't-test, AGI'], 1)` at $n=10$) and settles to
about 5% as $n$ grows, the Central Limit Theorem at work. **The variance
test does not settle.** It rejects a true null about
`{python} pct(robust.loc[30, 'variance test, AGI'], 0)` of the time at
$n=30$ and still `{python} pct(robust.loc[400, 'variance test, AGI'], 0)`
at $n=400$: four times the advertised rate, and a larger sample buys
nothing. The $F$ test, built from two sample variances, has the same
weakness.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**What to do about it.**

1. **Use the variance tests only for data you have reason to think are
   normal:** measurements from a stable process (fill weights,
   temperatures, machined parts), not incomes, sales, or waiting times with
   a long right tail. Check first: a histogram, and the Chapter 6 tail
   check.
2. **Do not use the $F$ test to choose between the pooled and Welch
   $t$-tests.** Your textbook suggests it (the rat Your Turn). The $F$ test
   is the *less* reliable of the two procedures, and choosing a test based
   on a pretest changes the error rates of the test you end up running.
   Use Welch, as in week 10. It is valid whether or not the variances are
   equal.
3. When a variance question matters on non-normal data, more robust
   methods exist (Levene's test in most software, or a bootstrap interval).
   They are beyond our textbook; ask Claude to run one and explain it.
:::

# Which Test Is It?

```{python}
#| label: catalog
pd.DataFrame([
    ("Are k proportions equal?", "counts of successes in k groups",
     "pooled p-bar times n_j", "k - 1", "right tail"),
    ("Do counts follow a stated model?", "counts in k categories",
     "n times model probability", "k - m - 1", "right tail"),
    ("Are two categorical variables independent?", "an r x c table of counts",
     "row x column / n", "(r - 1)(c - 1)", "right tail"),
    ("Is a variance equal to a claimed value?", "one sample, normal population",
     "(n - 1)s^2 / sigma0^2", "n - 1", "from H1"),
    ("Are two variances equal?", "two independent samples, normal populations",
     "F = s1^2 / s2^2", "(n1 - 1, n2 - 1)", "from H1"),
], columns=["question", "data", "statistic / expected count", "df", "tail"]
).set_index("question")
```

::: {.brown}
Name the test, state $H_0$, and give the degrees of freedom.

**(a)** A casino records which of four table games 400 guests chose, and
whether each guest was a loyalty member or not.

**(b)** A call center claims 50% of its calls arrive in the morning, 30% in
the afternoon, and 20% in the evening. A day's 600 calls are classified.

**(c)** A bottler's filling machine is specified to have a standard
deviation of no more than 0.15 ounces. Thirty bottles are weighed.

**(d)** Three Las Vegas hotels each survey guests on whether they would
return: 180 of 240, 150 of 220, and 200 of 250 say yes.

**(e)** The number of customer complaints per day over 90 days is tabulated
to decide whether a Poisson model can be used for staffing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

**(a)** Independence on a $2\times4$ table: $H_0$: game choice is
independent of membership; $\text{df}=(2-1)(4-1)=3$. It cannot show that
membership *causes* a game choice. **(b)** Goodness of fit with a stated
model: $H_0$: the shares are 0.5, 0.3, 0.2; $\text{df}=3-0-1=2$.
**(c)** One-variance test, upper tail: $H_0:\sigma^2\le0.0225$ against
$H_1:\sigma^2>0.0225$, with 29 df. Fill weights from a stable process are a
reasonable place to assume normality, but check a histogram. **(d)** $k$
proportions: $H_0:p_1=p_2=p_3$, $\text{df}=2$. **(e)** Goodness of fit with
$\lambda$ estimated by $\bar{x}$, so $m=1$ and $\text{df}=k-2$ after
combining the top categories until every expected count is at least 5.
Remember that a large p-value means "no evidence against Poisson," not
"Poisson confirmed."
:::

# Doing It in Excel

```{python}
#| label: crosswalk
chisq_crosswalk()
```

::: {.scarlet}
**Two Excel traps.** `CHISQ.TEST` returns a p-value directly from the
observed and expected ranges, but it always uses $k-1$ df for a single
column (or $(r-1)(c-1)$ for a table), so it is wrong for a goodness-of-fit
test in which a parameter was estimated. And the **Data Analysis → F-Test
Two-Sample for Variances** tool reports one-tailed results only, for the
populations in the order you entered them. For a two-tailed test, double its
p-value, or use `=F.TEST(range1, range2)`, which is already two-tailed.
:::

# Reading the Textbook: Corrections

::: {.scarlet}
1. **"A smaller chi-square test statistic … increases the likelihood that
   there is support for the null hypothesis"** (Section 12.1). A small
   $\chi^2$ means the data fail to contradict $H_0$. It is not support for
   $H_0$.
2. **Significance levels.** This course uses $\alpha=0.05$ for every
   test. Your textbook uses $\alpha=0.10$ for the drive-through, Southwest,
   and Canon Business Solutions examples (and the drive-through example then
   compares its p-value with 0.05 anyway). These notes restate all three at
   $\alpha=0.05$; none of the conclusions changes.
3. **Southwest's late flights.** "By rejecting the null hypothesis, we have
   no evidence to conclude that the number of late flights … follows the
   binomial distribution" is garbled: rejecting $H_0$ *is* the evidence that
   the binomial does not fit. And the book never says why it fails (weather
   makes a day's flights dependent; see the exercise above).
4. **"More evidence supporting the use of the Poisson distribution than
   there is to not use it"** ($p=0.94$), and similarly for the normal fit to
   SAT scores. A large p-value is not evidence for the model. The normal fit
   used 1 df on 40 scores and would miss almost any departure.
5. **`CHISQ.TEST` is presented as equivalent to `CHISQ.DIST.RT`.** It is
   only when no parameter was estimated ($m=0$).
6. **"Always assign the larger sample variance to Population 1"** (Section
   13.2). Fine for a two-tailed test; for a one-tailed test, the direction
   comes from the question (above).
7. **Using the $F$ test to decide whether to pool** (the rat Your Turn).
   Don't pretest; use Welch.
8. **The waiting-line *Focus on Analytics* box** gives a variance "of 7.2
   minutes" and says times "would vary by less than 7.2 minutes." A variance
   is in minutes²; the standard deviation is $\sqrt{7.2}\approx2.7$ minutes.
9. **Typos.** `CHI.DIST.RT` should be `CHISQ.DIST.RT`. The checkout
   example's hand-computed variance is misprinted; Excel's `VAR.S` value,
   2.1464, is correct.
10. **The refrigerator: "choosing to find support for the null
    hypothesis."** This is accepting $H_0$. The interval for $\sigma$ above
    shows how little 30 readings pin down.
11. **The book's normality warning is right and understated.** It calls the
    normal requirement "fairly rigid." The AGI simulation shows a nominal 5%
    test rejecting a true null about 21% of the time at every sample size.
:::

### Your own junior analyst

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> A hotel group surveyed 390 guests about the booking channel they used
> (direct website, online travel agency, phone, travel agent) and their
> trip purpose (business, leisure). The counts are: business = 92, 58, 24,
> 4; leisure = 88, 102, 16, 6 (in the channel order above). By running
> code, (1) test at alpha = 0.05 whether channel and trip purpose are
> independent, and check every expected count before trusting the p-value;
> if any is below 5, combine categories sensibly and test again;
> (2) show me the standardized residuals and tell me in plain English which
> cells drive the result; (3) report Cramer's V and say whether the
> association is weak, moderate, or strong; and (4) tell me whether these
> data show that trip purpose causes the choice of channel.
:::

Check four things in the reply: the expected count for business travelers
booking through a travel agent is below 5, so the reply should combine
"phone" and "travel agent" (or explain another sensible merge) before
concluding; the residual discussion names specific cells rather than
repeating "reject"; Cramér's V is reported with a verbal size; and the answer
to the last question says the survey is observational, so it shows
association only.

### Working in Excel

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> Build me an Excel workbook that shows why the variance test needs normal
> data. Sheet 1: in A2:A31, 30 values from a normal population with
> standard deviation 10, =NORM.INV(RAND(), 50, 10). In B2:B31, 30 values
> from a skewed population with the same standard deviation 10,
> =-10*LN(RAND()) (an exponential with mean 10 and standard deviation 10).
> At the top, for each column, compute the sample variance =VAR.S, the
> statistic =29*VAR.S(...)/100, and the two-sided p-value
> =2*MIN(CHISQ.DIST(x, 29, TRUE), CHISQ.DIST.RT(x, 29)), and a cell that
> says "reject" when the p-value is below 0.05. (Use formulas rather than
> the Data Analysis tool, whose output does not recalculate.) Give me the
> file to download.
:::

Press F9 forty times and count how often each column says "reject." Both
columns test a **true** null ($\sigma=10$). Which column rejects close to
5% of the time, and which rejects far more often? In one paragraph, explain
what this means for a manager who wants to use the variance test on waiting
times or sales.
